notes: BUG, NOT A QUIRK - floor(), ceil() and round() ARE BROKEN ON THE LIVE SITE AND YOUR PORT MUST REPRODUCE THAT. preprocess_math_expr rewrites every bare function name to math::<name>, but evalexpr 12.0.3 binds floor/round/ceil at the TOP LEVEL, not under math:: (see evalexpr-12.0.3/src/function/builtin.rs lines 86-88, alongside 'math::ln', 'math::sin', ...). So 'floor(x)' becomes 'math::floor(x)', which fails at eval time with `Function identifier is not bound to anything by context: "math::floor".` for EVERY sample. render_plot_svg still returns Ok(svg): you get axes, grid and labels but ZERO polylines. Golden: golden/broken_floor_no_curve.svg, 2773 bytes, polylineCount 0. Typing 'math::floor(x)' does not help either - the strip pass turns it back into 'floor' and the add pass re-prefixes it. If your port wires floor/ceil/round to the platform's real floor/ceil/round, it will draw a staircase where the site draws nothing, and every screenshot diff will fail.

format_label's integer branch TRUNCATES, it does not round. The test is `(val - val.round()).abs() < 1e-9` but the print is `format!("{}", val as i64)`, and `as i64` truncates toward zero. So any tick that lands a hair BELOW an integer prints the integer below it: 0.9999999999 -> "0" (not "1"), 2.9999999996 -> "2", -2.9999999996 -> "-2", 999.9999999999 -> "999", 123.99999999995 -> "123". This is not hypothetical: golden/tick_label_truncation.svg (x and y both [-5,-3]) has the tick sequence -5, -4.80, -4.60, -4.40, -4.20, "-3", -3.80, -3.60, -3.40, -3.20 - the accumulated -4.0 arrives as -3.9999999999999996 and prints as "-3", out of order, in the middle of the axis. Do NOT 'fix' this to Int(val.rounded()).

The grid/tick loops ACCUMULATE (`gx += x_step`) and you must accumulate too. Computing tick i as `start + i*step` is a different number. Evidence: for x in [-1,1], step 0.2, the accumulated sixth tick is -5.551115123125783e-17, which format_label renders as "-5.6e-17" - see golden/tick_drift_zero_label.svg, where BOTH axes are labelled -1, -0.80, -0.60, -0.40, -0.20, -5.6e-17, 0.20, ... A port that index-computes gets a clean "0" there and fails. Worse, drift can change the tick COUNT: golden/tick_drift_extra_tick.svg ([-0.9, 0.3], step 0.1) emits 13 ticks per axis; index-computing gives 12. The loop guard is `while gx <= x_max` on the accumulated value, so the last tick's presence is decided by accumulated error.

Rust's `{:.1e}` exponent format is NOT what any of your three target platforms produce by default. Rust prints the exponent bare - no sign, no zero padding: 1000 -> "1.0e3", 0.005 -> "5.0e-3", 1.0 -> "1.0e0", 1e300 -> "1.0e300". Measured on this machine: Swift String(format:"%.1e", 1000) = "1.0e+03"; Java/Kotlin String.format("%.1e", 1000.0) = "1.0e+03"; JS (1000).toExponential(1) = "1.0e+3". All three are wrong for this renderer. Build the string by hand: mantissa at 1 decimal place, the literal 'e', then the exponent as a plain signed integer with no padding and no leading '+'.

Rust's `{:.1e}` and `{:.2}` round half-to-EVEN on the exact binary value; Java/Kotlin's Formatter rounds half-UP and JavaScript's toFixed/toExponential round half-away-from-zero ('pick the larger n'). Measured divergences on this machine: 1250 -> Rust "1.2e3", Swift "1.2e+03", Java "1.3e+03", JS "1.3e+3". 0.125 -> Rust `{:.2}` "0.12", Swift "%.2f" "0.12", Java "0.13", JS toFixed(2) "0.13"; and Rust `{:.1e}` "1.2e-1" vs Java "1.3e-01" vs JS "1.3e-1". Swift goes through C printf and therefore MATCHES Rust's rounding (it only differs on exponent format); Kotlin and TypeScript need their own correctly-rounded formatter, not String.format / toFixed. Note that 1350 -> "1.4e3" on every platform, because 1350 is not a tie in binary (1.35 is stored as 1.350000000000000088...) - only exact ties expose the difference, which is why this bug survives casual testing. Compare against rustPrimitives.fmt_1e / rustPrimitives.fmt_2f in every formatLabel row, not just the final label.

EVERY comparison and boolean operator makes the plot EMPTY. The eval closure matches only `Ok(Value::Float)` and `Ok(Value::Int)`; `_ => None`. `x > 0` evaluates fine, to Value::Boolean(true) - and the closure throws it away and returns None, so nothing is drawn. Golden: golden/boolean_no_curve.svg, polylineCount 0. Using a boolean arithmetically is a different failure with the same result: `(x>0)*2` raises `Expected a Value::Float or Value::Int, but got Boolean(true).` -> None. There is NO boolean-to-number coercion anywhere. Same for strings ('"abc"'), tuples ('(1,2)') and Empty.

evalexpr has an integer type and integer division truncates. Literals without a decimal point are Value::Int: '5/2' is 2, not 2.5; '7/2' is 3; '-7/2' is -3 (truncation toward zero, not floor); '100/10/2' is 5 (left-associative). One float anywhere promotes the whole subexpression: '5.0/2' and '5/2.0' are both 2.5. Because x, pi and e are always bound as Value::Float, anything touching x is float - the Int path only bites on constant subexpressions. Golden golden/int_division_trunc.svg plots the constant '5/2' as a flat line at y=2. '%' is Rust's remainder, so -7%3 is -1 and 7%-3 is 1, NOT Python-style modulo.

Integer division and integer modulo BY ZERO are errors (-> None), but float division by zero is not. '1/0' raises `Error dividing 1 / 0` and '1%0' raises `Error modulating 1 % 0`, both giving None. But '1.0/0.0' is +inf, '0.0/0.0' is NaN, '-1.0/0.0' is -inf, '1.0%0.0' is NaN, and '1/x' at x=0.0 is +inf (x is a Float, so this is float division). The plot loop then discards inf and NaN via `y.is_finite()`, so both paths look the same on screen - but they are different code paths and the eval contract distinguishes them.

'^' is exponentiation, it is LEFT-associative, and it always returns Float. '2^3^2' is 64, NOT 512 - it parses as (2^3)^2. Every other calculator and most languages (Python, Ruby, Julia, math notation) make ** / ^ right-associative; if you reuse an off-the-shelf Pratt parser with the usual right-associative power rule your port will silently return 512. '^' also binds TIGHTER than unary minus: '-x^2' at x=3 is -9, and '-2^2' is -4. And '2^3' is Float(8.0), not Int(8), so '1+2*3^2' is Float(19.0) while '2+3*4' is Int(14).

preprocess_math_expr is a regex rewrite with three behaviours a naive string-replace will miss. (1) It DELETES whitespace between a function name and its '(' : 'sin (x)' becomes 'math::sin(x)' because the replacement template is 'math::$1$2' where $2 captured only the paren. (2) It is guarded by \b, so 'mysin(x)', 'x_sin(x)' and 'sinx' are left completely alone (and then fail as unbound identifiers). It is case-sensitive: 'SIN(x)' is untouched. (3) Alternation order is load-bearing and leftmost-first: 'asinh' precedes 'asin' precedes 'sin', 'atan2' precedes 'atan', 'exp2' precedes 'exp', 'log10' and 'log2' precede 'ln'. Reorder that list and 'asinh(x)' becomes 'math::asin' + 'h(x)'. Also: 'math::math::sin(x)' survives as a double prefix and fails, and the built-ins that are NOT in the fns list (min, max, if, len, typeof, math::log, math::is_nan, bitand, ...) pass through untouched - so 'min(x,0)' WORKS while 'log(8,2)' does not (only 'math::log(8,2)' does).

An EMPTY or whitespace-only expression is NOT a parse error. build_operator_tree("") succeeds and evaluates to Value::Empty, so the closure returns None and render_plot_svg returns Ok(...) - the user gets a clean, curveless chart, not the red 'Parse error:' message. Same for '()'. Do not add an is-empty guard that returns an error.

render_plot_svg wraps parse failures as `format!("Parse error: {}", e)` - the string your UI shows is 'Parse error: ' + evalexpr's own Display text, e.g. 'Parse error: Found an unmatched opening parenthesis '('.' (note the trailing period and the quoted paren). Only a handful of malformed inputs actually fail at PARSE time: unmatched parens, an unmatched double quote, and adjacent literals ('1 2' -> 'Tried to append a node to a leaf node.'). Almost everything else - 'x +', '@x', '1.2.3', 'foo(x)', 'x = 1', '[1,2]' - PARSES and fails at EVAL time, which the closure swallows into None. So a bad expression usually yields a silent empty plot, not an error message. Match the stage, not just the text.

The polyline break logic is asymmetric and easy to get subtly wrong. `first` starts true, so out-of-window samples BEFORE the curve enters the window emit nothing. A break only flushes when `!first`, so a run of consecutive out-of-window samples produces exactly ONE polyline, not one per sample. A run of length 1 DOES produce a polyline with a single point and no space: golden/single_point_run.svg contains `<polyline points="300.00,200.00" .../>`. NaN is handled by the same branch as out-of-range (`y.is_finite()` is false), and None (eval failure) by a separate but identical branch. Trailing points are flushed after the loop only `if !points.is_empty()`.

Window membership is tested on the RAW y with `y >= y_min && y <= y_max` - inclusive on both ends, and evaluated BEFORE any scaling. NaN fails both comparisons, so it breaks the run. Do not reorder this to test the scaled screen coordinate, and do not use an epsilon.

The SVG header numbers come from Rust's `{}` Display for f64, which prints 600.0 as "600", not "600.0": `viewBox="0 0 600 400" width="600" height="400"`. Swift's "\(600.0)" and Kotlin's 600.0.toString() both give "600.0"; JS String(600.0) gives "600". Hard-code the literal strings. Everything else is fixed-precision: grid/axis/rect coordinates use `{:.1}` ("40.0", "360.0") and polyline points use `{:.2}` ("40.00,156.48"), comma-separated within a point and space-separated between points, with no trailing space.

The empty axis group is ALWAYS emitted. When neither axis line is visible (y_min > 0 or y_max < 0, and likewise for x) the output still contains the literal `<g stroke="#999" stroke-width="1"></g>`. Golden: golden/no_zero_on_either_axis.svg ([1,3] x [1,9]). Do not skip the group when it has no children. The same is true of the grid group and the label group, which are never empty in practice but are unconditionally opened and closed.

nice_step's decade. The site computes it `10f64.powf(rough.log10().floor())`, and an earlier version of this note called that safe and told you to `Call pow.` THAT WAS WRONG, and it cost a red CI on md.vscode v1.2.0 (fd71a4e). MEASURED: `Math.pow(10,n)` differs from the decimal literal `1e<n>` for 68 of the 632 exponents in [-323,308] on Node 20 and Node 22, for 2 on Node 24, and for 0 on Node 26; OpenJDK 21's Math.pow(10.0,-5.0) is also one ULP off its literal. Darwin's libm happens to be correct, which is exactly why this survived review on a Mac. A wrong decade changes `norm = rough / mag`, which crosses a branch of the 1/2/5/10 ladder, which changes the tick step and therefore the DRAWN FIGURE - on Node 20 the recorded `tiny_range` figure comes out 16191 bytes instead of 16431. DO THIS INSTEAD: get the decade by parsing the decimal string "1e<n>" - Number() in JS, Double(_:) in Swift, String.toDouble() in Kotlin, str::parse in Rust - all of which ARE specified to be correctly rounded, and then pin the exponent by exact comparison (`if pow10(e) > rough { e -= 1 } else if pow10(e+1) <= rough { e += 1 }`) rather than trusting `log10().floor()`, which is not correctly rounded either. STILL TRUE, and the reason the original note existed: do NOT build the decade with a `r *= 10` / `r /= 10` loop. That gets a different double for 25 of the 61 exponents in [-30,30] - at n=-16 repeated division yields 1.00000000000000010e-16 where the literal is 9.99999999999999979e-17. A hand-typed table of literals is fine; a computed one is not. Every niceStep row carries intermediates.rough, intermediates.floorLog10Rough and intermediates.mag so you can bisect which step diverges. Note also that `rough.log10().floor()` is computed on the ALREADY-divided rough (range/8.0), not on range.

nice_step's branch thresholds are inclusive `<=` and sit on exact ties, so one ULP flips the answer. norm <= 1.5 -> 1.0; <= 3.0 -> 2.0; <= 7.0 -> 5.0; else 10.0. Range 12.0 gives rough exactly 1.5 and step 1.0, but 12.000000000000002 gives step 2.0. Range 24.0 -> 2.0, 24.000000000000004 -> 5.0. Range 56.0 -> 5.0, 56.00000000000001 -> 10.0. The final `else` branch (10.0) is reachable only when norm is in (7,10), e.g. range 64 -> step 10, range 640 -> step 100, range 0.064 -> step 0.01; golden/nice_step_ten_branch.svg exercises it on both axes. nice_step is also NOT guarded: nice_step(0.0) is 0.0, nice_step(-1.0) is NaN, nice_step(inf) is inf. render_plot_svg rejects those ranges earlier with `Invalid range: max must be greater than min`, so a port that guards inside nice_step instead will emit the wrong error.

Samples are computed as `x = x_min + (i as f64) / (steps as f64) * x_range` with steps = 1000, giving 1001 inclusive samples. The 'obvious' optimisation `x_min + i*dx` (dx = x_range/1000) is a DIFFERENT number for 221 of the 1001 samples on the default [-10,10] plot, and it does change rendered output: golden/sampling_formula_sensitive.svg ('x' over [-6.3, 0.7999999999999998] x [-3.3, 3.1]) contains the coordinate 348.47, which the i*dx formula turns into 348.48. Divide first, then multiply.

format_label's dispatch order is `val == 0.0` first, then `abs >= 1000 || abs < 0.01` (scientific), then near-integer, then `{:.2}`. Two consequences catch everyone. 999.999 has abs < 1000, so it does NOT go scientific - it goes to `{:.2}` and prints "1000.00", a four-digit label in the branch that is supposed to keep labels short. And 0.009999 has abs < 0.01, so it DOES go scientific and prints "1.0e-2", which reads as 0.01 - a value the non-scientific branch would have printed as "0.01" anyway. Also `val == 0.0` is true for -0.0, so negative zero prints "0" and never reaches the sign-preserving branches.

Non-finite values reaching format_label print Rust's spellings, and all three target platforms disagree with Rust somewhere. Rust: NaN -> "NaN" (via `{:.2}`, because NaN fails every earlier test including the near-integer one), +inf -> "inf" and -inf -> "-inf" (via `{:.1e}`, because inf.abs() >= 1000.0). Measured on this machine: Swift String(format:"%.2f", .nan) = "nan" (lowercase - WRONG) and "%.1e" of infinity = "inf" (right). Java/Kotlin String.format("%.2f", NaN) = "NaN" (right) but "%.1e" of infinity = "Infinity" (WRONG). JS gives "NaN" and "Infinity". These are unreachable through the tick loops on a valid range, but the formatLabel vectors pin them, so implement them literally. Relatedly, `val as i64` in Rust is a SATURATING cast (inf -> i64::MAX = 9223372036854775807, -inf -> i64::MIN, NaN -> 0); Swift's Int(Double) TRAPS at runtime on inf/NaN and Kotlin's .toLong() saturates like Rust - guard the cast even though the guarded path is unreachable.

x, pi and e are re-bound into a FRESH HashMapContext on every one of the 1001 samples, and they are plain variables, not reserved words. 'pi' is std::f64::consts::PI (0x400921fb54442d18) and 'e' is std::f64::consts::E (0x4005bf0a8b145769). Any other identifier is unbound: 'y' fails with `Variable identifier is not bound to anything by context: "y".`, and note that capital 'X' is NOT x. Assignment is rejected: 'x=1' fails with `Cannot manipulate context` because the tree is evaluated with an immutable context.

Arity is not checked at parse time and the error messages are type errors, not arity errors, because evalexpr passes a Tuple for multi-argument calls. 'sqrt(1,2)' -> `Expected a Value::Float or Value::Int, but got Tuple([Int(1), Int(2)]).`; 'sin()' -> `... but got Empty.`; 'hypot(3)' and 'atan2(1)' -> `Expected a Value::Tuple, but got Int(3).` All of them yield None from the closure. If your port validates arity up front you will produce different error text for the same input.

Comparison chaining is an error, not a fold: '1<2<3' fails with `Expected a Value::Number or a Value::String, but got Boolean(true).` The '!' operator requires a Boolean: '!x' fails with `Expected a Value::Boolean, but got Float(1.0).` and '!1' with `... but got Int(1).` '&&' and '||' likewise reject numbers. There is no truthiness anywhere in this language.

Numeric literal syntax is evalexpr's, not your platform's. '1e3' and '1E3' are Float(1000.0). '.5' and '5.' are valid Floats. '0x10' is Int(16). Integer literals are i64 and lose precision on the way to f64: '9007199254740993' becomes 9007199254740992.0. A literal that overflows i64 falls back to Float: '9223372036854775807' is Int, '9223372036854775808' is Float. '**' is not an operator ('x ** 2' parses as two multiplications and fails with `An operator expected 2 arguments, but got 1.`).

'x,' , ',x' and '(,)' all parse and evaluate to a Tuple containing Empty, so they are silent no-curve plots, not errors. So is 'x;y' - it parses, and fails at eval on the unbound 'y'. Treat the comma as a tuple constructor, not as an argument separator that only exists inside a call.

render_plot_svg's only Err path is the range check: `if x_range <= 0.0 || y_range <= 0.0` -> `Invalid range: max must be greater than min`. It fires BEFORE the expression is even parsed, so an invalid range beats a syntax error. Equal min and max is an error, not a degenerate one-pixel plot. See the svgErrors array.
